title: Blink, taken apart
dek: Chromium's rendering engine is 213,000 files, and 189,644 of them are web tests. This is a teardown of the rest: how third_party/blink is layered and how that layering is enforced, what runs on which thread, how a byte of HTML and a CSS property name become C++ classes, how one BeginMainFrame becomes pixels, and where Blink hands off to V8, to cc, and to //content. Everything is read at chromium/src@f288fed6 — Chrome 156.0.8067.0, 18 September 2026.
description: A teardown of Blink at chromium/src@f288fed6: layering, threads, the scheduler, bytes to pixels, Oilpan, bindings, runtime flags, web tests.
og_description: Chromium's rendering engine read end to end at commit f288fed6 (Chrome 156.0.8067.0): the tree and its DEPS-enforced layering, the process and thread model, the RenderingNG pipeline, Oilpan on cppgc, Web IDL bindings, runtime-enabled features and web tests.
twitter_description: Blink at chromium/src@f288fed6, taken apart: 213,000 files, a layering no build can violate, one main thread, twelve pipeline stages, and where the engine stops.

sections.title: What Blink is, and where it stops
figures: fig-blink-boundary · lane diagram (SVG) · the twelve RenderingNG stages across three lanes with a heavy rule at compositor commit
sections.brief:
Thesis: Blink is defined by its boundaries, not by a feature list, and the reader should leave this section knowing exactly which four things it delegates. Open by naming the subject line: everything in this post is read at chromium/src@f288fed6, chrome/VERSION 156.0.8067.0, checked out 2026-09-18, V8 15.6.19.

Facts to use, with sources. The self-definition, quoted verbatim: "Blink is the browser engine used by Chromium. It is located in `src/third_party/blink`" [src/third_party/blink/README.md:3-4]; the code policy is borrowed from //content — "only code that implements web platform features should live in Blink" [same file:10-11]. Kentaro Hara's "How Blink works" (2018) gives the job list (implement the specs, embed V8, request resources, build DOM trees, compute style and layout, embed the compositor) and warns that "Blink" names two things: the directory, and a project that also spans //content/renderer/ and //content/browser/ [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1aitSOucL0VHZa9Z2vbRJSyAIsAz24kX8LFByQ5xQnUg — sign-in only; single-sourced, say so]. The far boundary is the load-bearing sentence: Blink "encompasses all the phases of rendering prior to compositing, culminating in compositor commit" [https://developer.chrome.com/docs/chromium/blinkng]; everything after commit — layerize, raster, activate, aggregate, draw — is cc and Viz [https://developer.chrome.com/docs/chromium/renderingng-architecture]. It is not runnable alone: "Blink is implemented on top of an abstract platform and thus cannot be run by itself. The Chromium Content module provides the implementation of this abstract platform" [https://www.chromium.org/blink/]. The four delegations: V8 for JS and Wasm (renderer/DEPS allows `+v8` and only a narrow slice of //net [src/third_party/blink/renderer/DEPS:96-99,121]); cc for compositing ("In the renderer, Blink is the client" [src/cc/README.md:3-5]); //content for process, navigation and IPC plumbing, re-exported to Chrome, Android WebView and others through the Content API [src/content/README.md:4-7,64-68]; and increasingly nothing at all — "Blink can use Mojo and directly talk to the browser process. This allows removal of unnecessary public APIs and abstraction layers" [src/third_party/blink/renderer/README.md:184-187].

Figure fig-blink-boundary: a three-lane SVG (renderer main thread / renderer compositor thread / Viz process) carrying the twelve RenderingNG stage names — Animate, Style, Layout, Pre-paint, Scroll, Paint, Commit on the main lane; Layerize, Raster, Activate on the compositor lane; Aggregate, Draw in Viz — with the DocumentLifecycle state names overlaid on the Blink half and a heavy vertical rule at commit labelled "Blink's boundary". Data: dossier figure plan F1; `document_lifecycle.h`:49-82; the "12 stages" Numbers row. The caption must carry the correction that `core/layout/README.md`'s lifecycle list is stale — cite the header.

Owned elsewhere, do not spend words on: history and the fork (§02), file counts and DEPS (§03), thread details (§04), the Content API surface (§05), what happens inside each stage (§08 and §09). Badge every chrome-dev-docs claim "from the docs" and every path-and-line claim "from the tree". No code excerpt in this section.

sections.title: The fork, and the two rewrites since
figures: fig-lineage · timeline (SVG) · two stacked bands: architecture 1998—2026, and subsystem ship milestones
sections.brief: Thesis: Blink began as a subtraction, and has been rebuilt twice underneath a shipping product without ever stopping. Three movements: the 2013 fork, three bot-driven megacommits that produced today's filenames, and two decade-long projects (BlinkNG, Onion Soup). Facts, with sources. Adam Barth, 3 April 2013, announced "a new open source rendering engine based on WebKit", motivated because "Chromium uses a different multi-process architecture than other WebKit-based browsers, and supporting multiple architectures over the years has led to increasing complexity", promising to "remove 7 build systems and delete more than 7,000 files—comprising more than 4.5 million lines—right off the bat" [https://blog.chromium.org/2013/04/blink-rendering-engine-for-chromium.html]. Beta was 28.0.1500.20 on 23 May 2013, the release that shipped "Blink's new threaded HTML parser" [https://blog.chromium.org/2013/05/chrome-28-beta-more-immersive-web.html]; Stable was 28.0.1500.71 on 9 July 2013 "for Windows, Macintosh and Chrome Frame platforms", Android the next day, Linux only on 30 July with 28.0.1500.95 [https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/2013/07/stable-channel-update.html]. The cleanest primary evidence that M28 is the fork milestone is the release-tag DEPS: M27 pins `src/third_party/WebKit/Source` plus `Tools/DumpRenderTree` and `LayoutTests` (663 lines); M28 collapses all of it to a single `src/third_party/WebKit` pin (541 lines, zero DumpRenderTree references) [https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/refs/tags/28.0.1500.71/DEPS?format=TEXT] — badge the "M28 is the fork milestone" step reconstruction. The ``-tag naming story is hedged at source ("Rumor has it…") and has no 2013 primary [https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/blink]; print the hedge rather than the anecdote. The three megacommits: "Reformat blink" (clang-format, 1 Oct 2016, 1c8e1a7719e9), "The Blink Rename" to Chromium identifier style (9 Apr 2017, 1c4d759e4425) which kept web-exposed methods `namedLikeThis()`, and "The Great Blink mv" (7 Apr 2018, 0aee4434a4db) which moved `Source/` to `third_party/blink/renderer` with snake_case filenames. BlinkNG (from 2014) attacked "leaky abstraction barriers", reentrant entry points and layout running during style, replacing them with uniform entry, functional stages, immutable outputs and lifecycle assertions [https://developer.chrome.com/docs/chromium/blinkng]. Onion Soup started in November 2015 — the founding design doc is bylined "esprehn@, Nov. 2015", it was presented at BlinkOn 5 (San Francisco, 10–11 November 2015) and announced on blink-dev by Elliott Sprehn on 2015-12-09 under crbug.com/561879; Hara drove it from "Onion Soup 2.0" (2017) [https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/mE1IbfrKupY; .../platform-architecture-dev/c/L8D46_Yabyc]. Its definition: "migrate web-platform features from //content/renderer/ to Blink and massively simplify the abstraction layers". Attribute the famous number carefully (dossier correction C04): Hara recalled "64 directories in //content/renderer/", but measured release-tag counts are 29 at M47 and peak at 31 (M49/M50); 64 matches content/renderer + content/child + content/common combined. At f288fed6, //content/renderer is 7 subdirectories and 231 files [git ls-tree HEAD content/renderer/]. Figure fig-lineage: two stacked SVG timeline bands. Top, architecture: KHTML 1998, WebKit 2001, fork 3 Apr 2013, Stable 9 Jul 2013, BlinkNG 2014, Onion Soup Nov 2015, Reformat Oct 2016, Rename Apr 2017, Great mv Apr 2018, f288fed6 Sep 2026. Bottom, subsystem ships: Slimming Paint M45/M58/M67/M75/M94 with the CompositeAfterPaint tip-of-tree flip marked separately at 2021-10-27; LayoutNG 77/102/103/106/108; Oilpan branch 2013 → unified heap M74 → library M94 → pointer compression M106; Fontations 128/133/136/145. Data: dossier F13, Timeline table. Owned elsewhere: the tree as it stands (§03), Slimming Paint and LayoutNG (§09), Oilpan (§10), the launch process (§11). No excerpt.

sections.title: The tree, and the order it keeps
figures: fig-tree-and-order · treemap + stack rows (SVG, wide) · left: third_party/blink by file count; right: the layer cake with the DEPS line that enforces each edge
sections.brief:
Thesis: the layering is not a convention anyone remembers — it is enforced three ways, and no build can violate it. Lead with the scale, then show the enforcement.

Counts, all from `git ls-tree` at f288fed6. third_party/blink is 213,000 files, 42% of chromium/src (507,507) — but 189,644 of them are web tests (89% of Blink), of which 96,670 are under external/wpt and 28,217 are platform-specific baselines. The engine proper is renderer/: 18,997 files (7,124 .cc, 6,125 .h, 1,702 *_test.cc), split core 9,191 (css 1,165, html 1,056, layout 854), modules 5,163 across 121 feature directories, platform 3,783 across 38, bindings 588, build 182, controller 61, extensions 22. public/ is 1,560 files including 360 .mojom; common/ is 359. State plainly what this means: the thing people call "the engine" is about a tenth of the directory.

The order, quoted from renderer/README.md:119-129 — public/web → controller/ → extensions/ → modules/ and bindings/modules → core/ and bindings/core → platform/ → public/platform → public/common → //base, V8. Enforcement one: DEPS files per directory. platform/DEPS bans bindings, core and modules and enumerates the allowed base/ headers one by one [src/third_party/blink/renderer/platform/DEPS:2-4,97-99]; public/DEPS bans renderer internals and permits platform/heap and platform/wtf only inside INSIDE_BLINK [src/third_party/blink/public/DEPS:6-13]; controller/DEPS is the only layer with a blanket `+base` [src/third_party/blink/renderer/controller/DEPS:1-11]. Enforcement two: the presubmit — audit_non_blink_usage.py tolerates STL and GURL only for interop with blink/common, and disallows `base::BindOnce` in favour of `blink::BindOnce` [src/third_party/blink/tools/blinkpy/presubmit/audit_non_blink_usage.py:1012-1020,1115-1119]. Enforcement three: two clang plugins wired in renderer/BUILD.gn, the same file that defines INSIDE_BLINK [src/third_party/blink/renderer/BUILD.gn:33-50,104-121]. Say the quiet part the README says out loud: the core/modules/platform split is an implementation convenience — "specs do not have a notion of 'core', 'platform' or 'modules'" — with a rule of thumb (coupled to HTML/CSS/DOM → core; depends on core → modules; core depends on it → platform) [renderer/README.md:58-70]. Close on the threading policy and its stated reason: message passing only, because shared-memory patterns "have been one of the major sources of use-after-free security bugs" [renderer/README.md:190-201].

Two verbatim excerpts. X2, `src/third_party/blink/renderer/platform/DEPS`:1-4,94-100 — the ban list and the itemised base/ allowances. X9, `src/third_party/blink/public/platform/web_string.h`:43-45,167-177 — the same header presenting WTF types inside Blink and an opaque handle outside, which is the whole INSIDE_BLINK trick.

Figure fig-tree-and-order (wide): one SVG, two halves. Left, a treemap of third_party/blink by file count with web_tests dominating and renderer exploded into core/modules/platform/bindings/build/controller/extensions. Right, the layer cake drawn as downward-only arrows, each labelled with the DEPS line that enforces it, plus a side panel for the INSIDE_BLINK boundary. Data: dossier F2 and F3, and the Numbers rows for every count.

Owned elsewhere: the contents of public/ as an API (§05), bindings/ as a compiler (§07), platform/heap (§10), web_tests/ as a test system (§11).

sections.title: Processes, threads, and the scheduler
figures: fig-containers · nested-container diagram (SVG) · processes → threads in one renderer → main-thread object graph
fig-scheduler · ladder + timeline strip (SVG) · the scheduler hierarchy, the 11-rung priority ladder, and a backgrounded page's clock
sections.brief:
Thesis: Blink has one main thread, and the engineering is in the scheduler deciding what that thread may do next. Three movements: which process, which thread, which object.

Process. Blink runs only in sandboxed renderers; placement is a browser-side decision over SiteInfo (the principal, usually scheme+eTLD+1), SiteInstance ("roughly an agent cluster") and BrowsingInstance [src/docs/process_model_and_site_isolation.md:80-131]. Desktop is full site-per-process, Chrome 67, ~10–13% memory overhead; Android ≥ 2 GB is partial (Chrome 77, 3–5%); low-RAM Android, WebView and iOS none [same:141-195; https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/site-isolation/]. Since 127.0.6483.0 desktop isolates same-site sandboxed iframes too [same:453-459].

Thread. One CrRendererMain, one compositor thread. renderer_main.cc builds the scheduler before the sandbox engages [main content/renderer/renderer_main.cc:104-114,196]; RenderThreadImpl::InitializeWebKit spins a NonMainThread of ThreadType::kCompositorThread at base::ThreadType::kPresentation unless --disable-threaded-compositing [main render_thread_impl.cc:800-807; main platform/scheduler/common/thread.cc:76-107]. Each WorkerThread borrows a WorkerBackingThread with its own isolate and Oilpan heap; termination forcibly stops JS after a 2-second grace; pausing enters a nested run loop where only unpausable queues run [main core/workers/worker_backing_thread.h:22-25; worker_thread.cc:84; core/execution_context/PausingAndFreezing.md:54-61].

Scheduler, on base::sequence_manager. A task is a base::OnceClosure and tasks are atomic; almost everything must be posted through FrameScheduler::GetTaskRunner(TaskType), and SingleThreadTaskRunner::GetCurrentDefault is banned in blink/ and content/renderer/ [platform/scheduler/TaskSchedulingInBlink.md:23-34,38-47,69-77]. 79 TaskType values [public/platform/task_type.h:10-22,292-296]; FrameSchedulerImpl maps each to QueueTraits — deferrable, throttleable, intensively throttleable, pausable, freezable, plus a prioritisation type [main frame_scheduler_impl.cc:487-640]; 11 priority rungs, kControlPriority to kBestEffortPriority. Compositor priority follows a UseCase state machine (kEarlyLoading … kDiscreteInputResponse) over a UserModel with 100/300/2000/50 ms constants; rendering is starved after 100 ms, 500 ms under render-blocking loads [main use_case.h:13-54; user_model.h:21-39; main_thread_scheduler_impl.h:112-122]. Idle periods: < 10 ms short, ≤ 50 ms long, 1 ms minimum, still running 10 s after the renderer hides. Background policy with correction C01 stated exactly: 1 s wake-ups ten seconds after backgrounding, one per minute after a 5-minute grace (60 s once loaded); kDefaultDelayForBackgroundTabFreezing is base::Minutes(1), but renderer-side freezing is gated on blink::features::kStopInBackground, default-on only for IS_ANDROID && !IS_CAST_ANDROID && !IS_DESKTOP_ANDROID — elsewhere pages freeze only when the embedder calls PageSchedulerImpl::SetPageFrozen(). The doc's "five minutes" held from 2019 until M143 (fffc79af056c, 2025-10-06) [main page_scheduler_impl.cc:52-56,843-861; main third_party/blink/common/features.cc:2249-2261].

Object. blink::Page "roughly corresponds to a tab or popup" and owns a FrameTree; "a remote frame is always cross-site" [main core/page/page.h:112-119; public/web/web_frame.h:60-65]. Only local roots own a WebFrameWidgetImpl and therefore a cc::LayerTreeHost [public/web/web_local_frame.h:275-289]. LocalDOMWindow is the ExecutionContext — core/execution_context/README.md:10 is stale [main core/frame/local_dom_window.h:115-120]. One WindowAgentFactory per browsing context group hands out a WindowAgent per AgentClusterKey, each owning a scheduler::EventLoop and microtask queue [main core/execution_context/agent.h:27-59]. One isolate per main thread in shipping builds; MBI is disabled by default.

Excerpt: X17, task_priority.h:14-31 (chromium/main, fetched 2026-09-18).

Figures. fig-containers: nested SVG frames — browser + N renderers + Viz; inside one renderer CrRendererMain / Compositor / IO / workers; on the main thread AgentSchedulingGroup → WebView/Page → LocalFrame/RemoteFrame → LocalDOMWindow/Document with WindowAgent → EventLoop hanging off. fig-scheduler: hierarchy on the left, 11-rung ladder with UseCase arrows on the right, a bottom strip timing a backgrounded page. Data: dossier F4/F5.

Owned elsewhere: WindowProxy and the frames×worlds matrix (§07); the microtask queue's behaviour and the BeginMainFrame task (§08); the mojom surface and frame swaps (§05).

sections.title: The boundary with the embedder
figures: fig-input-path · three-lane sequence (SVG) · browser main → renderer compositor → renderer main, with the ack lane returning
fig-mirror · table ledger · browser object | mojom interface | renderer/Blink object | what crosses
sections.brief:
Thesis: public/ is a contract with exactly one consumer, and three flows cross it — input, navigation, loading. Write the flows; let the API appear inside them.

The contract. public/ is the whole public API; "everything else in Blink is an implementation detail"; the consumer is the content layer; there is no binary compatibility [src/third_party/blink/public/README.md:4-19]. Four parts: public/common (browser+renderer shared, STL-flavoured, no Web prefix), public/platform (the abstract blink::Platform Blink calls *down* into, implemented by renderer/platform/exported), public/web (WebView, WebLocalFrame, implemented by core/exported), public/mojom [same:24-67]. Print the sizes: 110 / 115 / 166 / 69 virtual declarations in platform.h, web_local_frame_client.h, web_local_frame.h, web_view.h; ~160 scalar fields in WebPreferences; 360 .mojom files in 150 directories. Boot: RenderThreadImpl::InitializeWebKit constructs RendererBlinkPlatformImpl, calls blink::Initialize(platform, binders, main_thread_scheduler), creates the compositor thread [public/web/blink.h:52-61]; CreateView → AgentSchedulingGroup::CreateWebView → WebView::Create with a self-owned WebViewClient, the PageBroadcast receiver and the agent-group scheduler [public/web/web_view.h:98-155]. RenderFrameImpl implements WebLocalFrameClient; WebLocalFrameImpl wraps LocalFrame; LocalFrameClientImpl forwards back out; ContentRendererClient is where Chrome, content_shell and WebView differ [content/public/renderer/content_renderer_client.h:96-122]. LocalFrame/LocalFrameHost carry 57 and 77 methods and are "handled directly in Blink without passing through content" [public/mojom/frame/frame.mojom:283-291,863-871]. Ordering is the subtlety: Mojo is FIFO per pipe only, so navigation-ordered messages ride channel-associated interfaces and must use TaskType::kInternalNavigationAssociated [src/docs/mojo_ipc_conversion.md:88-127; public/platform/task_type.h:246-259].

Input. RenderWidgetHostImpl::Forward{Mouse,Wheel,Keyboard,Gesture}Event → RenderInputRouter/InputRouterImpl (gesture, wheel, touch queues + TouchActionFilter) → blink.mojom.WidgetInputHandler::DispatchEvent [main components/input/input_router_impl.h:47-56; public/mojom/input/input_handler.mojom:560-577]. WidgetInputHandlerImpl is bound on the compositor thread "so that events stay in order"; InputHandlerProxy asks cc::InputHandler to ScrollBegin/Update/End and returns one of six dispositions [main input_handler_proxy.h:121-161]. Settle the contradiction (V28): the browser synthesizes GestureScroll events, the renderer compositor latches them. Otherwise: MainThreadEventQueue → WebFrameWidgetImpl::HandleInputEvent → WidgetEventHandler → blink::EventHandler → EventTarget::DispatchEvent, where EventPath::Initialize runs three passes — CalculatePath, CalculateAdjustedTargets (retargeting), and a numbering pass recording the nearest closed shadow tree so composedPath() can hide it [event_path.cc:90-231]. Blink pushes a 4×4 EventListenerClass × EventListenerProperties matrix to cc [src/cc/input/event_listener_properties.h:12-34]. Ack: DispatchEventResult (4) → WebInputEventResult (4) → InputEventResultState (7), with two caveats printed — HandleInputEvent returns kHandledSystem for every mousedown/mousemove/mouseleave regardless of what script did, and the click from pointerup is not merged into the mouseup result [widget_event_handler.cc:53-121; pointer_event_manager.cc:1272-1286]. kHungRendererDelay is 15 s desktop, 5 s Android.

Navigation and loading, compressed. FrameLoader::StartNavigation → WebLocalFrameClient::BeginNavigation → FrameHost::BeginNavigation; NavigationRequest walks 12 states to DID_COMMIT and calls NavigationClient::CommitNavigation with response head, body pipe, loader-factory bundle and policy container. RenderFrameImpl::CommitNavigation → WebNavigationControl::CommitNavigation → FrameLoader → DocumentLoader::CommitNavigation creates Document, DocumentParser and LocalDOMWindow; the renderer's ack is "the authoritative commit time" [src/docs/navigation.md:76-99]. Subresources are renderer-driven: ResourceFetcher per DocumentLoader, ResourceLoader per Resource, blink::URLLoader over a factory from the ChildURLLoaderFactoryBundle handed over at commit, on unfreezable task runners [platform/loader/README.md:5-24].

Excerpt: X44, `src/cc/input/input_handler.h`:301-309 — the latching contract.

Figures. fig-input-path: three SVG lanes with the ack returning along the bottom, annotating both caveats. fig-mirror: a table pairing browser object, mojom interface and renderer object for view, frame, widget, page, navigation. Data: dossier F6.

Owned elsewhere: task types (§04), dispatch versus microtasks (§08), the parser DocumentLoader creates (§06).

sections.title: How names become classes
figures: fig-front-doors · two-column sequence + number line (SVG, wide) · life of <div class=x> beside life of width: 50%, with the CSSPropertyID number line as a bottom strip
sections.brief:
Thesis: two text formats become C++ objects through one json5-plus-Jinja toolchain, and both id spaces are build artifacts — to read them you must run the generator. Three movements: toolchain, HTML front door, CSS front door. Toolchain is renderer/build/scripts, driven from scripts.gni [.../build/scripts/scripts.gni:124-163, 261-284].

HTML. html_tag_names.json5 lists 153 tags collapsing onto 90 distinct C++ classes — 47 are plain HTMLElement, 5 legacy tags map to HTMLUnknownElement; 13 sit behind runtime flags, 3 are origin-trialled. make_element_factory.py emits html_names.{h,cc} (one HTMLQualifiedName per tag, `enum class HTMLTag` with kUnknown = 0, TagToQualifiedName()) and html_element_factory.{h,cc}; make_element_lookup_trie.py emits LookupHtmlTag(), a 2,093-line switch on length then characters; make_element_type_enum.py emits ElementType (166 enumerators = 90 HTML + 64 SVG + 12 MathML) and the DowncastTraits behind IsA<HTMLDivElement> [templates/make_qualified_names.h.tmpl:27-57]. CoreInitializer reserves kQualifiedNamesCount = 968; html_names::kAttrsCount = 460 = 407 + 53 ARIA. At runtime: HTMLTokenizer (76 states) → AtomicHTMLToken, which calls LookupHtmlTag once and caches the tag and the AtomicString → HTMLTreeBuilder's `switch (token->GetHTMLTag())` over 21 insertion modes → HTMLConstructionSite::CreateElement, which resolves the custom-element registry for the intended parent and, when a definition exists, performs a microtask checkpoint, opens a CEReactionsScope and runs the author constructor synchronously before re-applying attributes [main core/html/parser/html_construction_site.cc:1222-1345]. Budgets, with their reason: 250 tokens (kDefaultMaxTokenizationBudget) plus 10 ms widening to 500 ms desktop / 50 ms Android after 6 / 2 yields, 1e7 for file:// and chrome-extension:// — "chosen using experiment data from the field to optimize Core Web Vitals". State the arc once (V25): threaded parser in Chrome 28, ForceSynchronousHTMLParsing default from M96, background parser deleted 2022-02-02 (4dbb35444d), kThreadedPreloadScanner still off — the 2026 parser is main-thread budget-and-yield.

CSS. css_properties.json5 is 11,136 lines, 75 documented parameters, 828 entries: 568 longhands, 141 shorthands, 119 aliases (106 -webkit-), 33 internal, 82 runtime-flagged. IDs sort on (-priority, internal-visited-first, name) from 2, so kColorScheme = 2 … kZoom = 43 are the 42 high-priority properties, kLastCSSProperty = 710, aliases 711–829, kNumCSSPropertyIDs = 830, the id field is 10 bits, kMaxShorthandExpansion = 19 because `font` expands to 19 longhands [css_properties.py:292-296,340-373; generated css_property_names.h]. Lookup is a gperf perfect hash over 825 (name, id) pairs where the 110 not unconditionally web-exposed carry kNotKnownExposedPropertyBit (0x8000), so the common case skips the exposure check [main core/css/parser/css_property_parser.cc:352-400; core/css/hash_tools.h:28-37]. make_css_property_subclasses.py emits 671 longhand and 157 shorthand `final` classes whose constexpr constructors bake the id, a 40-bit flag word and the separator into a 16-byte CSSProperty; make_css_property_instances.py lays them out in one alignas(16) union array indexed by CSSPropertyID [css_properties.h.tmpl:35-81; css_property_instances.h.tmpl:27-53]. Style-builder code is inline in longhands.cc (441 ApplyInitial and 424 ApplyValue bodies); ~50,978 generated lines for CSS alone.

Excerpts. X52, html_construction_site.cc:1224-1236, 1305-1339 — the custom-element branch. X57, css_property_parser.cc:352-400 — gperf with the exposure bit.

Figure fig-front-doors (wide): two SVG columns — life of `<div class=x>`, life of `width: 50%` — over a shared bottom strip drawing the CSSPropertyID number line (0 kInvalid | 1 kVariable | 2–43 high priority | 44–710 | 711–829 aliases) plus a 153-to-90 bar. Data: dossier F7/F8.

Owned elsewhere: cascade, ComputedStyle, UA sheets (§09); the IDL compiler (§07); runtime flags (§11).

sections.title: Bindings, contexts, and running script
figures: fig-idl-pipeline · pipeline diagram (SVG) · .idl → pickles → database (+ features json5) → 11 parallel actions → gen/v8_*, with one V8Foo exploded into its installers
fig-split-window · diagram (SVG) · one persistent outer proxy over successive inner globals; 7-link vs 2-link prototype chains; the frames×worlds matrix
sections.brief:
Thesis: the JS-facing surface is compiled, not written, and what a v8::Context costs was decided at build time. Three movements: compiler, context, script.

Compiler. idl_in_core.gni lists 892 files, idl_in_modules.gni 1,350; the tree holds 893 core .idl — the extra, core/css/css_nested_declarations_rule.idl, is not in the build list (V26) [bindings/idl_in_core.gni:7,874]. Pipeline: collect_idl_files.py (parse to IDLNode ASTs, pickle per component) → build_web_idl_database.py (IRs copied phase by phase: merge partials, merge mixins, process inheritance, assign v8::CppHeapPointerTag values, group overloads, compute exposure) → generate_bindings.py in 11 per-kind GN actions that parallelise on RBE [web_idl/README.md:54-89; idl_compiler.py:99-152; bindings/BUILD.gn:186-292]; 2,243 + 3,619 v8_* paths come out. The load-bearing detail: the database step consumes runtime_enabled_features.json5, so the compiler knows whether a [RuntimeEnabled] feature is "context dependent" [bindings/BUILD.gn:100-134; web_idl/runtime_enabled_features.py:47-73]. Each V8Foo carries a WrapperTypeInfo, InstallInterfaceTemplate, three installers (unconditional, context-independent, context-dependent) and InstallPropertiesPerFeature(ScriptState*, OriginTrialFeature) [bind_gen/interface.py:4312-4320,7385-7480].

Contexts. A ScriptState is 1:1 with a v8::Context and must never be stored on a DOM object, because DOM objects are reachable from multiple worlds and a leak between extension worlds is a severe security bug [main platform/bindings/script_state.h:34-41,71-78]. N frames × M worlds, created lazily [V8BindingDesign.md:185-199]; WindowProxyManager holds one eager main-world proxy plus a lazy map of isolated-world ones [window_proxy_manager.h:65,80-81]. The split window is V8's JSGlobalProxy plus a prototype chain Blink wires: outer global proxy → inner global object → Window.prototype → WindowProperties → EventTarget.prototype → Object.prototype → null, against a two-link RemoteWindowProxy chain where every access hits the cross-origin interceptors [window_proxy.h:105-129]; six lifecycle states. The inner global is 1:1 with a Document except for the documented initial-about:blank reuse, which DocumentLoader::ShouldReuseDOMWindow() gates on origin access and matching cross-origin-isolation keys — the case that keeps a window.open() caller's synchronous modifications alive [window_proxy.h:64-68; main core/loader/document_loader.cc:2663-2684]. What a context costs is answered by the build-time snapshot: two contexts (main world with a cached HTMLDocument wrapper, one isolated world) plus 2×6 FunctionTemplates — Window, WindowProperties, HTMLDocument, Document, Node, EventTarget — generated with all runtime features off because "it's easier to add properties than removing ones", and linked with ICF disabled because identical-code folding breaks the 1:1 external-reference mapping [v8_context_snapshot_impl.cc:62-92,117-149,418-452]. The 2017 intent claimed 1.6–3× faster context init; 1.6 MB of Android binary kept it desktop-only.

Script. PrepareScript → ClassicPendingScript (kWaitingForResource → kWaitingForCacheConsumer → kReady) → ExecuteScriptBlock → V8ScriptRunner::CompileAndRunScript, which computes (CompileOptions, ProduceCacheOptions, NoCacheReason) and runs under a V8RunMicrotasksScope and a 44-deep recursion guard [main core/script/pending_script.cc:301-316; v8_script_runner.cc:76-78,469-512]. Streaming is decided in layers with a histogram-stable 30-value NotStreamingReason enum; with BackgroundResourceFetch on by default it starts from the loader's background thread [script_streamer.h:53-95]. The code cache is Blink-managed metadata on the HTTP-cache entry, tagged code (0) / timestamp (1) / compile hints (2) in 2 bits: under 1024 characters is never cached, a timestamp is "hot" under 72 hours, and production happens *after* top-level execution so lazily compiled functions are included [v8_code_cache.cc:36-77,360,466-541].

Excerpts. X80, window_proxy.h:105-125 — the prototype chain, in the header's own comment. X66, idl_compiler.py:99-152.

Figures as listed; data from dossier F9/F10.

Owned elsewhere: runtime flags and origin trials (§11); microtask timing (§08); ScriptWrappable as a GC edge (§10).

sections.title: One frame, unrolled
figures: fig-begin-main-frame · timeline (SVG, wide) · one ProxyMain::BeginMainFrame band by band, with a spec-step row, a runs-script? row, and a microtask-trace inset
sections.brief:
Thesis: "update the rendering" is a task cc posts into Blink, and everything the spec calls the event loop happens inside it or between two of them. Three movements: tasks, microtasks, the frame.

Tasks. The spec's per-event-loop task queues do not exist. Quote it: "in our implementation, a frame has task queues. This is an intentional violation of the specification. Therefore, currently, EventLoop is a unit that just manages a microtask queue" [main scheduler/public/event_loop.h:40-46].

Microtasks. Each blink::Agent owns a scheduler::EventLoop wrapping a v8::MicrotaskQueue created as v8::MicrotaskQueue::New(isolate, kScoped), per agent since M108 (CL 3928076; kill switch removed 2023-08-16), bound to every window context on both the v8::Context::New and FromSnapshot paths [main core/execution_context/window_agent.cc:12-16; main local_window_proxy.cc:349-352]. Two checkpoints: V8 drains when the outermost kRunMicrotasks scope exits, and MainThreadSchedulerImpl::OnTaskCompleted checkpoints before anything else, because microtasks may detach the queue that just ran [v8_initializer.cc:884-889; main main_thread_scheduler_impl.cc:2611-2619]. This is why microtasks run between two listeners of a browser-dispatched event but not when script calls el.click() — and (C03) that is not an inference: the HTML spec says it in a note under "clean up after running script", and Jake Archibald demonstrated it in 2015. Three caveats: Blink's V8RunMicrotasksScope wrapper (2026-03-03, 1be1a11d01) degrades to kDoNotRunMicrotasks while microtasks are paused; ~MicrotasksScope skips the drain when an exception is pending; kScoped is set on the isolate default queue and per agent.

The frame. Anything dirtying rendering calls LocalFrameView::ScheduleAnimation → ChromeClientImpl → WidgetBase → LayerTreeHost::SetNeedsAnimate [main local_frame_view.cc:4039-4047]. At the next viz BeginFrame, if SchedulerStateMachine::ShouldSendBeginMainFrame passes, ProxyImpl posts ProxyMain::BeginMainFrame to the agent-group scheduler's compositor queue (TaskType 38), whose priority is dynamic — kVeryHigh after 100 ms of starvation, kExtremelyHigh after 500 ms render-blocking, kHighest after discrete input [src/cc/scheduler/scheduler_state_machine.cc:505-552; src/cc/trees/proxy_impl.cc:806-851]. Inside that one task the order is fixed [src/cc/trees/proxy_main.cc:341-377]: compositor scroll deltas, mutator events, WillBeginMainFrame, BeginMainFrame (rAF-aligned input, then Page::Animate → ServiceScriptedAnimations), AnimateLayers, RequestMainFrameUpdate → UpdateLifecycle(kAll) → UpdateAllLifecyclePhases, UpdateLayers, WillCommit, the blocking commit, DidBeginMainFrame → RunPostLifecycleSteps. ServiceScriptedAnimations is written against the spec's step numbers — 6 reveal, 7 autofocus, 8 resize, 9 scroll, 10 media queries, 11 animations, 12 fullscreen, rVFC, 14 rAF — and since a Feb 2023 rewrite runs each step for all documents before the next [main core/page/page_animator.cc:205-351]. Steps 16–21 are UpdateLifecyclePhasesInternal: a loop of style+layout, pre-paint, IntersectionObserver and ResizeObserver delivery — the one place author script runs inside the lifecycle, wrapped in AllowUserAgentScript — until nothing dirties layout; then paint [main local_frame_view.cc:2515-2563,2650-2668]. The spec task has 23 top-level steps as of 2026-09-21. Spare numbers: TimeClamper 100 µs / 5 µs (fine only when cross-origin isolated); setTimeout clamps to 4 ms past nesting level 6.

Excerpts. X96, event_loop.h:40-57. X101, src/cc/trees/proxy_main.cc:354-377 — the fixed order.

Figure fig-begin-main-frame (wide): one SVG timeline of the task, band by band, with a second row giving each band its HTML spec step number and a third flagging "runs script?", plus an inset comparing two microtask traces (browser click with two listeners; el.click() from script). Data: dossier F11/F12.

Owned elsewhere: what each lifecycle phase computes (§09); priorities and throttling (§04); how rAF-aligned input arrived (§05).

sections.title: Style, layout, and pixels
figures: fig-property-trees · diagram (SVG, wide) · a small page → four property trees → display items → paint chunks → PendingLayer merge decisions
fig-to-pixels · sequence diagram (SVG) · PaintArtifact → cc layer list → commit → tiles → CompositorFrame → SurfaceAggregator → draw, as data structures, not threads
sections.brief:
Thesis: BlinkNG made every stage a function from immutable inputs to immutable outputs, and that is what lets the next stage cache. Five movements: lifecycle, style, layout, pre-paint and paint, out to Viz.

Lifecycle. The active path: kVisualUpdatePending → kInStyleRecalc/kStyleClean → kInPerformLayout/kAfterPerformLayout/kLayoutClean → kInCompositingInputsUpdate/kCompositingInputsClean → kInPrePaint/kPrePaintClean → kInPaint/kPaintClean [main core/dom/document_lifecycle.h:49-82]. Cite the header; core/layout/README.md is stale.

Style, three phases: index rules into RuleSet buckets keyed by the right-most compound selector; match through ElementRuleCollector/SelectorChecker; fold declarations through StyleCascade into an immutable ComputedStyle generated from the same css_properties.json5 [core/css/style-calculation.md:36-43,89-96,158-173]; Apply runs at most 15 times. Invalidation is set-based: RuleSets compile InvalidationSets; mutations mark nodes immediately or schedule sets pushed depth-first before recalc [core/css/style-invalidation.md:122-152]. html.css is 2,655 lines, ~340 rules, 52 @supports blink-feature() blocks and the UA-only __qem unit, parsed once per renderer and intentionally leaked; 19 IDR_UASTYLE_* resources ship, the rest lazy [main css_default_style_sheets.cc:98-137,375-400]. External sheets defer declaration parsing, skipping blocks with a SIMD scan called ~10× faster than tokenizing.

Layout is LayoutNG: an algorithm takes (BlockNode + ComputedStyle, ConstraintSpace, BreakToken) and returns a LayoutResult wrapping an immutable PhysicalFragment; results cache on the LayoutBox keyed by constraint space, which returned flex and grid to O(n) [layout/layout_ng.md:17-38,75-95]. Milestones: 77 block/inline/floats/out-of-flow, 102 fragmentation, 103 flex and grid, 106 tables, 108 printing, after which "the legacy engine is no longer used to perform layout" — carry the next sentence too (C06): legacy data structures still back offsetLeft/offsetTop. The NG prefix is gone tree-wide. Text gets one paragraph: ComputedStyle → FontDescription → Font → FontCache → SimpleFontData/SkTypeface; RunSegmenter cuts runs of constant script, orientation and emoji presentation; HarfBuzzShaper shapes windows of the whole paragraph with full context against FontFallbackIterator's 7 stages; NGShapeCache holds 2,048 entries of ≤ 30 code units. "In Chrome 145 we removed FreeType from Blink", corroborated by freetype.gni changing between tags 144 and 145.

Pre-paint walks the layout tree once, invalidating paint and building the four property trees — transform, clip, effect, scroll — into per-FragmentData ObjectPaintProperties with 42 node slots [core/paint/README.md:215-222; graphics/paint/README.md:38-42]. Paint walks the fragment tree in Appendix E order across five phases through one PaintController; display items group into chunks sharing a PropertyTreeState, and the immutable PaintArtifact is the next paint's cache.

Out. CompositeAfterPaint makes layerization post-paint: PaintArtifactCompositor builds PendingLayers and merges them unless a direct compositing reason, overlap or sparsity (kMergeSparsityAreaTolerance = 10000 px² × dpr²) forbids it; worst case is O(n²). cc commits the layer list to a pending tree, rasterizes 256×256 software tiles or GPU tiles stacked four high, activates, and builds a CompositorFrame that Viz's SurfaceAggregator merges before SkiaRenderer draws [src/docs/how_cc_works.md:238-282,334-360]. Get Slimming Paint right (C07): M45 → M58 → M67 → M75 → M94, "following launch, 22,000 lines of c++ were removed", −1.3% CPU and 3.5%+ p99 scroll as lower bounds for 2015–2021 — but M94 is the Finch milestone; the tip-of-tree default landed 2021-10-27 (1479240c28d2).

Excerpts: X126 document_lifecycle.h:49-82; X132 layout_algorithm.h:43-59.

Figures as listed; data from the PL numbers rows.

Owned elsewhere: parsing and tokenizing (§06); the frame driving this (§08); where Blink stops (§01).

sections.title: Oilpan, and what is left of WTF
figures: fig-heap-map · diagram (SVG) · the 4 GiB cage, size-bucketed spaces, large-object space, six custom spaces, a 128 KiB page with the 8-byte header, and a compressed-Member inset
fig-handles · table ledger · the eight handle types by where allowed, keeps alive, cleared on death, traced, write barrier
sections.brief:
Thesis: Blink's garbage collector is no longer in Blink, and the directory that remains is an adapter. Four movements: the carve-out, what cppgc is, the bridge to JavaScript, and what is still PartitionAlloc.

Carve-out. platform/heap is a 42-file layer whose type surface — GarbageCollected, Member, Persistent, Visitor — is 27 `using` aliases onto V8's cppgc, wrapping roughly 5.9k lines of Blink-specific glue: ThreadState, six custom spaces (two compactable backing spaces plus Node, CSSValue, LayoutObject and, since June 2026, Element), heap collections over WTF, and trace traits [src/.../heap/garbage_collected.h:24-31; member.h:21-28; custom_spaces.h:22-59]. The project ran from early 2020, launched in V8 v9.4, was enabled in Blink in M94, and "heap: Remove Oilpan in Blink" (2021-09-24, commit 0e8ab8bb7a15) deleted 23,206 lines of in-tree GC [https://v8.dev/blog/oilpan-library]. Allocation throughput after the switch: 40,660 → 46,451 alloc/ms on Linux, 32,038 → 34,559 on Windows. Scoping correction (C08): "~30k targets" is pre-carve-out motivation and ">400 unit tests" scopes stand-alone cppgc, not Blink.

cppgc. Mark-sweep with conservative stack scanning, incremental and concurrent marking and sweeping. 128 KiB pages (2^17), a 64 KiB large-object threshold, an 8-byte HeapObjectHeader (32-bit padding, 14-bit GCInfoIndex, in-construction bit, 15-bit size, mark bit), and a 4 GiB cage (16 GiB with CPPGC_ENABLE_LARGER_CAGE) that lets Member be a 32-bit compressed offset, shift 1 or 3. Pointer compression became the default in Chrome 106 for −21% P50 / −33% P99 Oilpan memory on Windows, −6% / −8% on Android [https://v8.dev/blog/oilpan-pointer-compression]; concurrent sweeping (M78) cut main-thread sweeping 25–50%, 42% on average.

Bridge. ScriptWrappable derives from v8::Object::Wrappable (itself cppgc::GarbageCollected) and stores its main-world wrapper inline as a TraceWrapperV8Reference, with other worlds' wrappers in DOMDataStore's ephemeron map — so a V8 major GC marks one combined graph rather than two [main platform/bindings/script_wrappable.h:47-53; dom_data_store.h:218-226]. That is the sentence that makes "who owns a DOM node" answerable.

WTF, and the correction worth printing. StringImpl's header is three 32-bit words — refcount, length, 24-bit hash plus 8 flag bits — followed by an inline LChar or UChar array; AtomicString interns into a per-thread table; PartitionAlloc's buffer and fast-malloc partitions carry under 10% worst-case bucket padding. The allocator decision is a five-way flowchart: script-exposed → Oilpan; lifetime simpler with GC → Oilpan; very high allocation rate and no cycles → PartitionAlloc (USING_FAST_MALLOC); stack-only → STACK_ALLOCATED; part-object → DISALLOW_NEW. Then say what the docs still get wrong (C02): wtf/Allocator.md:109-113 and wtf/allocator/Allocator.md:5-9,36-38 still put LayoutObjects on PartitionAlloc and describe a "LayoutObject partition". LayoutObject has been GarbageCollected since 2021-08-13 (reland #4, 77d6cb6241, bug 1030176) and allocated in LayoutObjectSpace (kSpaceIndex = 4, a space that predates the conversion — added 2021-03-31 by 5c902fed1aa0); LayoutPartition, the last ThreadUnsafePartition, was deleted 2021-12-06 (cc3b7598a441). Only the LayoutObject half of that sentence is stale — Strings are still on PartitionAlloc's buffer partition.

Excerpt: X156, `src/third_party/blink/renderer/platform/heap/member.h`:21-28,70-78 — the alias onto cppgc and the size assertion.

Figures as listed; data from dossier F14 and the memory figure ideas.

Owned elsewhere: wrappers as a bindings concern (§07); LayoutObject as a layout concern (§09); worker heaps (§04).

sections.title: Flags, tests, and shipping a feature
figures: fig-feature-stack · stack rows · the four gates a feature passes (chrome://flags → base::Feature/Finch → RuntimeEnabledFeatures::XEnabled(context) → origin-trial token) beside the status→where-it-runs matrix and the counts
sections.brief:
Thesis: in Blink a feature's existence is a row in a json5 file, its reach is a status string, and a line in TestExpectations is how the project admits it is not done. Three movements: the flag, the tests, the social process.

The flag. runtime_enabled_features.json5 is 7,514 lines and declares 1,227 features — use the corrected C10 tuple: 564 plain-string "stable", 301 "experimental", 90 "test", 90 per-platform status dictionaries (22 defaulting to stable), 182 with no status; 95 carry origin_trial_feature_name, 188 base_feature:"none", 79 depends_on, 26 implied_by, 3 custom_enable_check [json5 parse of src/third_party/blink/renderer/platform/runtime_enabled_features.json5 at f288fed6]. Status buys reach: none is on nowhere, test in content_shell web tests, experimental adds --enable-experimental-web-platform-features, stable is everyone [RuntimeEnabledFeatures.md:20-29]. make_runtime_features.py expands it into one `bool feature_states_[kFlagIndexCount]` array indexed by a uint16_t enum, name lookup by binary search over a NUL-separated string pool, accessors folding in depends_on and implied_by, and — only for origin-trial features — a FeatureEnabled(const FeatureContext*) overload [templates/runtime_enabled_features.h.tmpl:29-100]. Tokens are base64 structures of one version byte, a 64-byte Ed25519 signature, a 4-byte length and a JSON payload [public/common/origin_trials/origin_trials_token_structure.md:10-61]. Print the contradiction, do not resolve it: launching-features says an initial trial may run 12 milestones with 6-milestone extensions; running-an-origin-trial says "up to 6 milestones (~24 weeks)". Neither page is dated.

The tests. run_web_tests.py drives content_shell --run-web-tests. TestExpectations is 9,228 lines, 6,817 non-comment, 6,398 crbug-tagged, 5,219 referencing external/wpt/, 1,449 referencing virtual/. 194 virtual test suites re-run base directories with extra flags; the one to show is `stable` — owner blink-api-owners@, expires "never" — which runs the webexposed global-interface listings with --stable-release-mode, and is how an accidental change to the shipped API surface gets caught [web_tests/TestExpectations; main web_tests/VirtualTestSuites:3179-3222]. Bot shape: 5 / 2 / 1 / 18 shards for blink_web_tests, blink_wpt_tests, chrome_wpt_tests and headless_shell_wpt_tests, 3 retries, 5× timeout for [ Slow ]. WPT is two-way synced by LUCI cron builders; since the September 2024 PSA the WPT half is migrating from content_shell to wptrunner (2000+ regressions per platform reported at the time); CLs over 1,000 files are not exported; upstreaming typically takes 24 hours [src/docs/testing/web_platform_tests.md:258-395].

The social process. ChromeStatus entry → Intent to Prototype (no LGTM) → Ready for Developer Testing → optional Intent to Experiment (1 LGTM) → Intent to Ship (3 LGTMs) from the API owners listed in third_party/blink/API_OWNERS — 10 current, 8 emeritus in a 24-line file; 5 days before escalating a blocked intent to blink-api-owners-discuss@; roughly 2 milestones of soak before the RuntimeEnabledFeatures entry is removed [https://www.chromium.org/blink/launching-features/; API_OWNERS:1-24]. The point to land: three gates are machine-checked, one is a vote, and the json5 row connects them.

Excerpt: X69, runtime_enabled_features.json5:501-530 — one real entry, so the reader sees the row everything else is generated from.

Figure fig-feature-stack: stack rows (hl-blue → hl-green → hl-purple → hl-orange) for the four gates, a right-hand column carrying the counts (1,227 / 95 / 188 / 90), and beneath it the status→where-it-runs matrix. Data: BF figure ideas 4/5 and numbers rows.

Owned elsewhere: the IDL compiler's use of this file (§07); the generator toolchain (§06); Finch-gated scheduling (§04).

sections.title: What it teaches
sections.brief:
Thesis: five properties make a 19,000-file engine tractable, and each is a mechanism in this tree, not a slogan. No figure; no new facts. Every claim here must be a callback to a fact already established earlier in the post, cited again in short form.

One: boundaries are enforced by tooling. A layering diagram nobody can violate, because DEPS allow-lists, the audit_non_blink_usage.py presubmit and two clang plugins reject the commit, and INSIDE_BLINK makes one header present two APIs (§03). The lesson is the inversion — the document describes what the build enforces, not the other way round.

Two: stages are functions. BlinkNG's uniform entry, functional stages, immutable outputs and lifecycle assertions turned "when may I read this?" into an assertion on DocumentLifecycle, and immutability is what makes the caches sound: a LayoutResult keyed on its ConstraintSpace, a PaintArtifact that is its own cache for the next paint (§09). Caching is downstream of immutability, not a bolt-on.

Three: generate what repeats. 828 CSS properties, 153 tags, 2,242 build-listed IDL files and 1,227 feature flags are json5 rows compiled into C++ by generators in renderer/build/scripts and renderer/bindings/scripts — about 50,978 generated lines for CSS alone (§06, §07, §11). State the cost honestly: you cannot read the tree without running the generator, and this post had to.

Four: migrations end with a deletion. Slimming Paint over five milestones, ending in 22,000 removed lines; LayoutNG over six, ending with the legacy engine no longer performing layout; the Oilpan carve-out ending in 23,206 deleted lines; Fontations ending in "In Chrome 145 we removed FreeType from Blink" (§02, §09, §10). None of these ended with two code paths kept "just in case". That is the difference between a rewrite that lands and one that accretes.

Five: documentation decays faster than code, so cite the code. List the stale in-tree docs this teardown had to route around, with paths: core/execution_context/README.md:10 (Document inherits ExecutionContext), core/layout/README.md:9-14 (the lifecycle state list), wtf/Allocator.md:109-113 and wtf/allocator/Allocator.md:5-9,36-38 (LayoutObject on PartitionAlloc), TaskSchedulingInBlink.md:139-146 (five-minute freezing), platform/fonts/README.md:165-203 (the word cache), docs/how_cc_works.md:40. Each was true when written; each is now a trap. The practical rule this post followed: quote headers and source files with line numbers, quote docs only for intent.

Close on what is still open, briefly and without hedging into mush: whether MBI is enabled in any shipping build; whether kThreadedPreloadScanner has ever been Finch-enabled; which of the two origin-trial durations is current; the milestone in which SVG text moved onto LayoutNG. Then one sentence on what the whole teardown is for — an engine this size is legible only because its boundaries, its stages and its generated surfaces are all things a machine can check, and that is a transferable design decision, not a Chromium peculiarity.

Tone: this is the only section allowed to generalise, and it still carries paths. No marketing register, no "powerful", no "elegant". Keep it to six short movements and stop.

sections.title: Sources
sections.brief:
Thesis: make the provenance auditable. A grouped <ul> of sources, each with "— what it was used for", then the closing .footnote.

Group A, the subject. /home/coder/chromium-ref/src at chromium/src@f288fed6c601ae22461c9c9d8189004050abfaeb, chrome/VERSION 156.0.8067.0, checked out 2026-09-18; V8 15.6.19 [v8/include/v8-version.h]; depot_tools. Note that the checkout is sparse, so some files were read from the GitHub mirror of chromium/main on 2026-09-18, 09-21 and 09-22.

Group B, in-tree documents actually quoted, by path: third_party/blink/README.md; renderer/README.md; public/README.md; renderer/platform/DEPS, public/DEPS, renderer/controller/DEPS; renderer/BUILD.gn; tools/blinkpy/presubmit/audit_non_blink_usage.py; docs/process_model_and_site_isolation.md; platform/scheduler/TaskSchedulingInBlink.md; core/execution_context/PausingAndFreezing.md; docs/mojo_ipc_conversion.md; docs/navigation.md; platform/loader/README.md; bindings/scripts/web_idl/README.md; bindings/core/v8/V8BindingDesign.md; platform/RuntimeEnabledFeatures.md; public/common/origin_trials/origin_trials_token_structure.md; core/css/style-calculation.md; core/css/style-invalidation.md; core/layout/layout_ng.md; core/layout/block_layout.md; core/paint/README.md; platform/graphics/paint/README.md; platform/graphics/compositing/README.md; docs/how_cc_works.md; docs/testing/web_platform_tests.md; wtf/text/README.md; API_OWNERS; web_tests/TestExpectations; web_tests/VirtualTestSuites.

Group C, Chromium and V8 publications: the Blink launch post (2013-04-03); the Chrome 28 beta and stable release posts; BlinkNG and RenderingNG on developer.chrome.com; the RenderingNG fragmentation article; chromium.org/blink, /blink/slimming-paint/, /blink/launching-features/, /blink/guidelines/api-owners/, /blink/origin-trials/running-an-origin-trial/; Site Isolation on chromium.org; v8.dev on the Oilpan library, pointer compression, high-performance C++ GC, code caching and compile hints; developer.chrome.com/blog/memory-safety-fonts; the HTML Living Standard's event-loop processing model.

Group D, threads and commits: blink-dev mE1IbfrKupY and d8LMrlnba8o; platform-architecture-dev L8D46_Yabyc, 2De10giTga8 and nWgolZEdmIA; paint-dev PNOQR4gwfrY; the release-tag DEPS for 27.x and 28.0.1500.71; commits 1c8e1a7719e9, 1c4d759e4425, 0aee4434a4db, 0e8ab8bb7a15, 77d6cb6241, cc3b7598a441, 1479240c28d2, 4dbb35444d, fffc79af056c, 5c902fed1aa0, 1be1a11d01.

Then the provenance footnote, which must say four things explicitly. (1) What is sourced from the tree at f288fed6 and is exact. (2) What came from the GitHub mirror of chromium/main on 2026-09-18/21/22 because the sparse checkout omits it — those line numbers may drift by a few lines from f288fed6. (3) What is reconstruction: the "M28 is the fork milestone" reading of the release-tag DEPS, and any figure that composes facts from several files. (4) What was not verified: the four Google Docs behind sign-in, including "How Blink works" (last updated 2018-08-14) and "Life of a Pixel", so every architecture claim sourced to them is single-sourced; the field state of MBI, kThreadedPreloadScanner, kInputOnViz and cppgc's young generation; which origin-trial duration page is current; the milestone in which SVG text moved onto LayoutNG; the milestone at which Oilpan became always-on; and line-of-code counts, because the clone is blob-less and only file counts are available.

Keep the list to one entry per source with a short purpose clause. Do not restate findings here.
